This log documents how Codex assisted with project planning, data preparation, and R troubleshooting. It records selected prompts from the project conversation, follow-up instructions, resulting work, and remaining verification. It is a curated record rather than a complete chat transcript. Last updated: October 29, 2026. The final analysis is complete; earlier status notes describe the work at the time of each exchange.

## Category exploration and a more specific prompt

**Initial prompt:**

> Using the Inference folder, give me all the categories that can answer the research question:
>
> Where can someone find the best restaurants in a selected category in New Orleans, and which geographic area is best for finding them?

**Follow-up prompt:**

> Using the Inference folder, give me all the categories from the raw data folder that can answer the research question:
>
> Where can someone find the best restaurants in a selected category in New Orleans, and which geographic area is best for finding them?

The follow-up specified that the category list should come from the local raw data. Codex read the assignment instructions and extracted category tokens from the complete business JSON, restricting the inventory to New Orleans restaurant businesses. It produced a category inventory with counts and suggested related themes. The inventory contained 2,259 restaurants and 300 comma-separated category tokens, including incidental labels attached to restaurant records.

**Evidence:** [Category inventory](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/CATEGORY_INVENTORY.md) and [CSV inventory](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/data/new_orleans/category_inventory.csv). Counts reflect the documented filtering and comma-splitting rules; tokens are not guaranteed to be separate canonical Yelp categories.

## Selecting the theme and changing the ranking size

**Prompt:**

> Lets use the theme "New Orleans cooking" as the analysis. Lets go with the top 15 restaurants. We can decide on the geographical areas after filtering the data

The user selected the theme and changed the target from the assignment's top 10 to **top 15**. Codex implemented the theme using the previously proposed categories: **Cajun/Creole, Seafood, Southern, and Soul Food**. Inclusion requires at least one of those exact category tokens, together with the `Restaurants` token, city `New Orleans`, and state `LA`. Each business counts once in the combined group.

Codex wrote the import and cleaning workflow in `R/import.R` and `R/clean.R`. The import reads the complete JSON files in pages, retains the necessary columns, and saves filtered RDS files. It retained **672 theme restaurants and 250,304 reviews**. Both open and closed businesses were retained initially.

**Verification performed:** Codex loaded the saved RDS files with a separate R process, checked business and review ID uniqueness, confirmed that reviews link to the selected businesses, and verified that every selected restaurant has reviews and coordinates. These checks do not establish the best restaurants or current operating status.

**Evidence:** [Selection decisions](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/CATEGORY_SELECTION.md), [filter summary](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/data/new_orleans/cooking_filter_summary.json), [import code](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/R/import.R), and [cleaning code](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/R/clean.R).

## Clarifying geographic coverage and selecting comparison systems

**Clarification prompts:**

> WHat do you mean by geographic coverage and best restaurants or areas?

> Can you give me a list of all the geographical coverages?

Codex explained the difference between identifying individual restaurants and comparing areas. It listed the five systems in the assignment: ZCTAs, census tracts, census block groups, Neighborhood Statistical Areas, and wards.

**Decision prompt:**

> lets use ZIP codes and Wards

The user selected the two geographic systems to compare. Codex recorded **ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs) and New Orleans wards** in the project files. ZCTA assignment will use restaurant coordinates and boundary polygons rather than Yelp postal labels alone.

**Status at that stage:** Boundary data acquisition, spatial joins, area summaries, and verification of the seven-area requirement were pending. The later entries document their completion and the choice of wards.

## Missing-value checks and troubleshooting a failed command

**Initial prompt:**

> How do i manuall look for missing values? I did a quick skim but it seems like there are no missing values

Codex suggested counting `NA` values with `colSums(is.na(restaurants))`, checking blank text fields separately, and inspecting incomplete rows in RStudio. The first response assumed an object named `restaurants` already existed in the active session.

**Follow-up reporting the error:**

```text
> colSums(is.na(restaurants))
Error: object 'restaurants' not found

> colSums(is.na(name))
Error: object 'name' not found
```

Codex corrected the loading instructions and explained that `name` is a column inside the restaurant data frame. It provided this sequence:

```r
restaurants <- readRDS(
  "data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans_cooking.rds"
)
colSums(is.na(restaurants))
sum(is.na(restaurants$name))
```

It also suggested `readRDS(file.choose())` if the relative file path failed. This follow-up made the instructions usable in a fresh R session.

**Follow-up verification:** During the initial analysis requested below, Codex ran the full NA and blank-text checks. There were no NA values in the retained columns, but seven restaurant addresses were blank. The affected businesses were exported for follow-up and retained because their coordinates were present. A quick skim is not recorded as proof of completeness.

## Starting the descriptive analysis

**Prompt:**

> Can you start the analysis for me?

Codex implemented and ran `R/analysis.R` using the saved theme RDS files. It generated column-level missingness checks, validation checks, a business-level summary joined to available reviews, category summaries, and three plots. It also compared alternative restaurant review-count thresholds and reviewer activity thresholds without choosing a final cutoff.

The checks found no duplicate IDs, orphan reviews, restaurants without reviews, out-of-range ratings or coordinates, unparseable review dates, or invalid open-status values. There were seven blank addresses. The median published business rating was 4 stars; available reviews per restaurant ranged from 5 to 7,673. These checks do not establish location accuracy or current opening status.

Codex visually inspected the three exported plots and added the results to the report. At that stage, final rankings and geographic comparisons were pending. The code and tables are available in [the analysis script](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/R/analysis.R) and [the restaurant summary](https://github.com/Brandonlee-2002/Yelp_new_orleans/blob/main/data/analysis/restaurant_summary.csv).

## Completing steps 3–6 and auditing deliverables

**Prompt:** "Can you finish steps 3 to 6? Double check what else needs to be done as well."

Codex checked the instructor's steps, documented category counts and co-occurrence, and saved an explicit review-level many-to-one join with unchanged row counts and no unmatched businesses. It downloaded Census 2020 place/ZCTA boundaries and the official City of New Orleans ward layer, then used `sf` spatial joins to compare coverage.

The official city check identified 16 theme businesses outside Census New Orleans. Codex preserved them in a mismatch audit and selected 656 city-contained restaurants (249,002 reviews) for a like-for-like geographic comparison. Both systems had 17 populated areas. Wards were selected for the main comparison based on sample-size balance, with ZCTAs retained as a comparison. Two lakefront points approximately 13–16 metres outside the nearest ward remained unassigned; no snapping was used. Saved boundaries, source metadata, and checksums document the input versions.

Codex generated full-city and detail maps, count and raw-rating plots, area summaries, and a requirement-by-requirement audit. The next steps remain reviewer normalization, ranking eligibility and sensitivity, the top-15 table/map, final conclusions, and a tested package lockfile. Initial descriptive results retain the original 672-restaurant scope and are clearly separated from the stricter geographic results.

## Completing the analysis and professional presentation

**Prompt:** "finish all the remaining steps. make the pages look professional"

Codex completed the city-only reviewer analysis, calculating both mean and median reviewer baselines. The primary specification uses reviewers with at least five reviews in the selected city/category pool. Restaurant eligibility requires a snapshot-open flag, at least 50 total reviews, and at least 20 distinct eligible reviewers. The stricter reviewer-evidence threshold retains 288 restaurants versus 304 at a ten-reviewer minimum. Alternatives test reviewer activity, restaurant review volume, distinct-reviewer counts, median baselines, raw-star ranking, and area sample-size minima of five, ten, and fifteen restaurants. An initial ten-reviewer trial ranked Cafe Porche and snowbar first on eleven eligible reviewers. The final minimum was raised to twenty to avoid a headline recommendation with that little reviewer evidence; this cutoff was chosen after exploration, and the ten-reviewer alternative remains in the sensitivity table.

The final historical top 15 is led by Tito's Ceviche & Pisco, Ajun Cajun, and Restaurant August. Ward 9 leads the primary area comparison, which requires at least ten eligible restaurants per ward. Its lead is not stable across all specifications, so the report presents a conditional recommendation rather than a universal winner. Ward 13's nine eligible restaurants are explicitly shown below the area sample-size cutoff.

Codex added the final ranked table, a numbered ward-boundary map, raw/adjusted comparisons, area scores and sensitivity tables, conclusions, and reproducibility checks. The visual presentation uses shared navigation, typography, colors, summary cards, readable tables, and separate report, methods, and AI-log pages. The user selected the theme, top-15 target, and comparison systems; Codex selected and justified the final analysis thresholds. These are analytical choices, not user-provided criteria.

The environment audit found a dependency mismatch: the installed units package required a newer Rcpp. A compatible copy was installed in a temporary library, leaving the system library unchanged. A populated lockfile and an isolated restore test verified 50 package versions (47 project packages and three R-recommended packages) and regenerated the identical ordered top-15 IDs. Data and rendered-output checks are recorded alongside the analysis; historical operating status and the true causes of boundary mismatches have not been independently verified.


## Presenting the results as a visual story

**Prompt:** "could we show the results into a visual story? it would look more appealing? would that be more professional?"

Codex created a five-chapter visual narrative from the completed outputs: the restaurant selection funnel, an illustrative reviewer-baseline comparison, the top-15 ranking, the ward map, and ten area-sensitivity tiles. The full analytical report remains available on a separate Results page. Colors, labels, sample sizes, and uncertainty notes explain the evidence rather than imply new findings. Scenario counts are explicitly distinguished from probabilities or independent votes. The statistical outputs and ranking rules were preserved.


## Adding motion to the visual story

**Prompt:** "can you integrate any animations into the visual story?"

Codex added one-time scroll reveals, staged selection-bar growth, light card feedback, chapter highlighting, and a reading-progress indicator. Decorative motion follows the operating system's reduced-motion preference and can be turned off using a visible control. Numbers and statistical results remain fixed; no counting animation changes the displayed evidence. All content is readable without JavaScript, and the animation enhancement is confined to the visual-story page.


## Giving each chapter a distinct motion treatment

**Prompt:** "Can you have each section have a unique type of animation?"

Codex assigned content-specific, one-time animations: horizontal growth for selection bars, opposing slides for reviewer examples, staggered card entrances for standouts, an aperture reveal for the static ward map, and a row-by-row hinge reveal for sensitivity tiles. Chapter headings retain a quiet fade. Pause/cancel and reduced-motion behavior apply to every treatment. Map locations, numeric evidence, and the statistical outputs remain fixed.
